entities.name: Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela in Galicia, northwestern Spain, built over the believed tomb of St. James the Apostle beginning in the 9th century and substantially in its current Romanesque form between 1075-1211 CE, is one of the three great pilgrimage centers of medieval Christianity (alongside Rome and Jerusalem) and the destination of the Camino de Santiago (Way of St. James) — the most famous pilgrimage route in the Western world, which has experienced a remarkable modern revival with over 400,000 pilgrims completing it annually.

The Pórtico de la Gloria (1168-1188 CE) by Master Mateo — the cathedral's western sculptural portal — is one of the supreme achievements of Romanesque sculpture: 200 figures carved in a single integrated program depicting Christ in Majesty, the Last Judgment, Old and New Testament figures, and the Apostles with a psychological expressiveness and technical virtuosity that anticipated Gothic sculpture by decades. Pilgrims traditionally place their hands in the grooves worn into the central column (now protected with barriers) and knock their heads against the seated figure of Master Mateo himself — the 'Saint of Bumps' — hoping for his intelligence.

Santiago de Compostela's role in medieval European history extended far beyond religious pilgrimage: the cathedral and the Camino were among the primary transmission routes for cultural exchange between the Iberian Peninsula and the rest of Europe during the 11th-13th centuries. The pilgrimage route spread Romanesque architectural styles, musical traditions (including polyphony), and commerce across France and Spain. UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1985.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Santiago de Compostela Cathedral — one of the three great pilgrimage centers of medieval Christianity, the Pórtico de la Gloria's sculptural masterpiece, the destination of the Camino de Santiago (400,000+ annual pilgrims), and a primary cultural transmission route between medieval Iberia and Europe — is one of the most historically consequential religious monuments in Western Christendom.
